frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains state control over its gas sector and valuable pipeline links to Europe, but export dependence exposes it to European demand shifts and pricing pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya complicates Algeria’s border security and limits its room to balance regional diplomacy against outside military influence.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and debt
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and oil-linked financing continue to shape Angola’s fiscal options, even as Luanda seeks broader Western and Gulf investment.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor connecting Atlantic ports to critical-mineral regions is attracting U.S., European, and Chinese interest, increasing Angola’s bargaining power but also external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Niger transit rupture
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and complicated the use of Benin’s port and export infrastructure, with downstream effects on regional sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-financed logistics and energy projects are strengthening Benin’s connectivity while increasing exposure to external operators, commercial terms, and regional political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its importance to the diamond supply chain to demand greater domestic value capture, but remains exposed to De Beers’ market position and global diamond weakness.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited water availability and reliance on imported or carbon-intensive power could constrain industrial diversification and increase dependence on regional infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold production, challenging foreign mining interests while risking lower investment and weaker technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Closer security ties with Russia reduce reliance on Western partners but create new external dependency, while insurgent attacks continue to limit effective control over resource-producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral activity remains vulnerable to informal networks, opaque licensing, and cross-border smuggling. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture full value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tensions linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and strained relations with neighbors expose Burundi to external security demands and diplomatic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in ports, logistics, and maritime services strengthens connectivity but can create long-term dependence on outside operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on tourism, imported fuel, and external climate finance leaves the islands exposed to external economic shocks despite relatively strong institutions.

highlights: Oil, gas, and timber remain externally contested

frictionVectors.title: Resource-contract asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in oil, gas, mining, and timber continues to provide capital while limiting transparency and domestic value capture. Infrastructure and commodity access remain closely tied to external commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside insecurity in the Far North, weakens state control over transport corridors and resource-producing areas. Regional instability also increases dependence on external security and humanitarian support.

highlights: Security partnerships trade access for protection

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-resource nexus
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security actors has strengthened regime protection but increased concerns that mining access, concessions, and political influence are exchanged for military support.

frictionVectors.title: Weak corridor sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks retain influence over roads, gold fields, and border trade. Poor transport infrastructure makes the country dependent on neighboring states and external partners for market access.

highlights: Oil finances a highly centralized state

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to public finance, leaving Chad vulnerable to volatile prices and unequal bargaining with international operators. Limited diversification constrains genuinely sovereign economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: External security entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Chad's position along the Sahel and Sudan corridors sustains demand for foreign military and diplomatic engagement. Security partnerships provide regime support while creating leverage over strategic infrastructure and regional policy.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, making the territorial dispute a persistent sovereignty issue for Moroni. The dispute also affects maritime boundaries, migration policy, and access to surrounding resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign financing, remittances, and development assistance for ports, energy, and transport. Gulf, French, and broader international involvement brings investment but limits autonomous policy space.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial control, with Rwanda-linked armed networks and regional diplomacy shaping outcomes. Displaced populations and insecure mining zones weaken the state's ability to govern resource corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to competition among Chinese firms, Western governments, and Gulf-linked investors. The state is seeking better terms and supply-chain control, but infrastructure gaps and weak enforcement preserve substantial external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and export earnings remain heavily exposed to offshore oil prices and foreign operating partners. This constrains diversification and leaves national resource control vulnerable to external capital and market cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects have expanded connectivity while increasing concerns over debt, project transparency, and strategic dependence. The Pointe-Noire corridor remains vital to trade and foreign influence.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Commodity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening local processing and state oversight, but foreign traders and volatile global prices still shape producer incomes and export value. Land pressure and labor concerns add friction to the sector's long-term legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and logistics network attract French, Chinese, Gulf, and other international capital, creating growth opportunities alongside strategic dependence. Instability in the Sahel is also increasing pressure on northern borders and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Base Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but the arrangement narrows strategic autonomy and raises escalation risks. Competition among external powers makes the country a high-value pressure point.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Ethiopian Access
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports remain Ethiopia's principal maritime outlet, giving the government major bargaining power while creating dependence on Ethiopian trade flows. Debt exposure and Chinese participation in port infrastructure continue to generate sovereignty and refinancing concerns.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt, foreign-exchange shortages, and IMF-linked reforms increase Gulf and Western leverage over strategic assets and state-linked enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Suez security
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and attacks on shipping threaten Suez Canal revenues while Egypt balances maritime security coordination with sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and limited transparency leave the state exposed to foreign operators, volatile prices, and shrinking fiscal space.

frictionVectors.title: Gas infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional gas monetization and LNG ambitions require external capital and technology, constraining Malabo's control over future energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining partner dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production depends on foreign technical and financial partners, creating leverage despite strong state control over licensing.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, maritime powers, and neighboring states increase pressure on Eritrea's ports and security choices.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade corridors, customs revenue, energy supplies, and investment remain heavily tied to South Africa and the Southern African regional system.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and textile exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export industries depend on preferential market access and externally controlled supply chains, limiting domestic leverage over value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable maritime access remains a major source of friction with Somalia and regional governments, with outside powers competing for influence.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on foreign lenders constrain policy space, even as Addis Ababa seeks greater control over energy and transport assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and other minerals, but foreign operators still dominate capital, technology, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Railways, ports, and resource corridors remain vulnerable to external financing and management influence, particularly from Chinese and European-linked firms.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal border and fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Cross-border trade and security cooperation with Senegal are essential, while fishing access and maritime enforcement remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on external financing and contractors for port, electricity, and transport infrastructure, limiting independent control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and gold leakage
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated mining is damaging water systems and agricultural land while weakening state control over gold production and enabling foreign-linked trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions narrow policy space for industrial subsidies, infrastructure spending, and assertive renegotiation of mining and energy agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium dominance
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project promises major state revenue and infrastructure, but Chinese, Singaporean, and Western-linked consortiums retain decisive control over finance, technology, and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite enclave dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on foreign firms for bauxite extraction and export, with limited domestic refining and persistent disputes over taxation, land, and local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends on raw cashew exports and external buyers, leaving farmers and the state exposed to price manipulation, informal trade, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and illicit-network exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime and customs capacity makes ports and coastal routes vulnerable to transnational trafficking, while foreign partners retain substantial influence over security and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders remain important to transport and energy projects, creating exposure to refinancing pressure and contract leverage. Nairobi is increasingly balancing new borrowing against demands for greater transparency and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains strategically important, but competition from regional corridors and foreign-backed logistics projects could dilute Kenya's control over trade flows. Regional security risks also raise costs along the Northern Corridor.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and associated infrastructure are economically vital, but the relationship leaves Maseru heavily dependent on South African financing, markets, and security cooperation. Delays and cost disputes around major water projects increase this asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Hydropower and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower offers strategic autonomy but remains vulnerable to drought, limited transmission capacity, and dependence on regional electricity markets. Foreign contractors and financiers retain substantial influence over project delivery.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and emerging resource projects are dominated by large foreign operators, leaving Liberia dependent on concession revenue while facing persistent demands for stronger local processing and labor benefits. Fiscal capacity limits Monrovia's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port infrastructure are closely tied to mining investors and neighboring-country transit arrangements. This can prioritize enclave exports over broader national infrastructure and industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Foreign Security Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, and Western states continue to shape Libya's security and political environment through rival partnerships. Foreign military access and arms relationships constrain a coherent national resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Institution and Export Contest
frictionVectors.details: The National Oil Corporation and central revenue mechanisms remain vulnerable to factional pressure, blockades, and competing claims over spending authority. Hydrocarbon output is therefore both Libya's main source of leverage and its principal channel of external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining operations provide export earnings but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles, imported inputs, and limited domestic refining. The government faces pressure to improve royalties, environmental safeguards, and local procurement without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, ports, and power supply remain vulnerable to financing gaps and unreliable domestic infrastructure. Chinese, Gulf, and Western commercial interests compete for influence while the state struggles to convert projects into broad-based industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms constrain policy autonomy while Malawi remains exposed to donor and creditor conditions. Foreign-exchange shortages continue to affect fuel, fertilizer, and essential imports.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic mining competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium and other mineral projects could strengthen export revenues, but limited domestic processing capacity risks leaving value capture with foreign operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Mining control and fiscal confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and greater control over foreign mining firms, creating tensions with established operators and investors. Production and exports remain vulnerable to insecurity and regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian military assistance has reduced Western leverage but increased dependence on an external security provider. The partnership carries reputational, financial, and sovereignty risks amid persistent jihadist violence.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential but exposes Mauritania to foreign operators, offshore infrastructure risks, and bilateral disagreements over revenue and governance.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports and proposed green-hydrogen projects depend on long transport and port corridors. Security threats, water constraints, and foreign capital concentration could limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations involving the United Kingdom and the strategic Diego Garcia base. Any settlement must balance territorial control with major security and economic interests.

frictionVectors.title: External capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: The financial, port, and tourism sectors rely heavily on international investors and market access. Competition among India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners requires careful protection of regulatory autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding ports, renewable energy, and phosphate-linked infrastructure in Western Sahara while seeking wider international recognition of its sovereignty. The issue remains a persistent source of friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some international legal and commercial actors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment balancing
frictionVectors.details: Large European, Gulf, Chinese, and American investments are strengthening Morocco's logistics and industrial base but create exposure to external supply chains and strategic influence. Rabat is managing this through diversified partnerships and local-content policies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique's gas future remains dependent on foreign operators, export finance, and external security support. Delays around major LNG projects limit domestic leverage over the resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten energy infrastructure and transport corridors. Rwanda and other external security partners remain important to maintaining project access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and green-hydrogen projects could expand state revenues, but development is heavily reliant on international firms, finance, and technology. Local-content rules will determine how much value remains in Namibia.

frictionVectors.title: Export Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Ports, power, water, and rail capacity remain constraints on scaling new resource industries. Competition for logistics access with regional neighbors may increase as projects advance.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Benin have exposed Niger's dependence on cross-border infrastructure to monetize crude exports. Political control over the pipeline route remains a major sovereignty and revenue risk.

frictionVectors.title: Security and External Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's break with France and closer security ties with Russia have increased political autonomy while reducing access to Western financing and technical support. Persistent jihadist violence continues to constrain practical state control over mining areas.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: The Niger Delta still suffers from theft, vandalism, and community conflict, weakening federal control over production and export revenues. International operators are reducing exposure or shifting toward less risky assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western capital remains important for rail, ports, power, and energy projects. Financing can accelerate infrastructure delivery but may create long-term concession and debt exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral trading and its alleged support for M23 have triggered intense diplomatic pressure from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Western partners. Sanctions, traceability demands, and reputational risk could constrain the country's mineral-export model.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains strong administrative control but remains reliant on external aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment for infrastructure and industrial expansion. This limits full autonomy despite its centralized policy execution.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies on foreign firms and licensing partners to assess potentially commercial offshore hydrocarbons. Limited state capacity constrains bargaining power and environmental oversight.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing threatens a major national resource base. The country depends on external maritime surveillance and enforcement support in the Gulf of Guinea.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE CONTRACT REVIEW
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture from oil and gas projects while avoiding production disruption or investor flight. Tensions with international operators and lenders remain manageable but persistent.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY INFRASTRUCTURE BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Export terminals, domestic gas distribution and power infrastructure must expand quickly to convert hydrocarbons into broad-based sovereignty gains. Foreign capital and technical expertise remain indispensable.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles has strong incentives to protect tuna stocks and its extensive maritime zone, but enforcement depends on foreign patrol, satellite and intelligence support. Commercial fishing access can create sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: STRATEGIC PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European and Gulf actors compete for influence through port, logistics and security cooperation. Victoria must balance these relationships without allowing infrastructure dependence to narrow its diplomatic autonomy.

highlights: Energy and logistics gaps limit value capture

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINING CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports, while foreign operators control much of the capital, technology and logistics. The state faces continuing pressure to improve royalties, local processing and transparency.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND POWER DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors and electricity supply depend heavily on external finance and operators. Weak infrastructure reduces domestic bargaining power and limits the economy-wide benefits of resource extraction.

highlights: Offshore hydrocarbons are a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: OIL LICENSING AND FEDERAL TENSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed offshore exploration offers major upside but risks intensifying disputes between the federal government and member states over ownership, revenue sharing and licensing authority. Weak institutions make contract oversight especially vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, BASES AND MARITIME INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states and other external actors provide security and infrastructure while competing for access to strategic ports and maritime routes. Somalia gains capacity but risks fragmented control over critical assets.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, aging transmission assets, and constrained freight rail weaken South Africa's ability to process and export minerals on sovereign terms. Private capital and foreign technology remain important to restoring capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-beneficiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Government is seeking greater local processing of platinum-group metals, manganese, and other critical minerals, but investors resist rules that could raise costs or limit export flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenue depends on infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving production exposed to conflict, damage, payment disputes, and external operators. This sharply limits sovereign control over its principal resource.

frictionVectors.title: Elite-linked resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and weak institutions allow oil proceeds and contracts to be shaped by competing elites and foreign intermediaries. Delayed political reforms further deter transparent infrastructure and investment planning.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and trade-route competition
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and external networks contest gold production, taxation, and export routes, reducing civilian and state control over revenues. The conflict also invites covert foreign support tied to resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea port system, oil infrastructure, and transport corridors remain vulnerable to disruption and political capture. Dependence on external logistics, finance, and security relationships constrains Khartoum's future bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-finance balancing
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is diversifying partners across China, Gulf states, India, and Western institutions for rail, port, and energy projects. The resulting leverage improves options but raises concerns over debt terms, concessions, and long-term control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Local-processing and tighter licensing policies seek to capture more value from gold, graphite, nickel, and other minerals. Implementation remains vulnerable to investor pressure, regulatory capacity gaps, and informal extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor concentration
frictionVectors.details: Togo's trade sovereignty is concentrated in the Port of Lomé and its links to landlocked Sahel markets, making customs revenue and logistics vulnerable to foreign operators, financing conditions, and regional disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and border insecurity in the northern corridor threaten transport, agricultural supply chains, and state presence. Expanded external security assistance may improve protection while increasing dependence on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial influence over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance to externally conditioned assistance limits room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Grid Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains reliant on imported Algerian gas and European-linked energy infrastructure. Renewable projects could improve autonomy, but financing and implementation remain externally dependent.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and Foreign Oil Control
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's upstream oil and export plans are led by foreign firms and depend on the Tanzania-linked EACOP corridor. Environmental litigation, land disputes, and financing pressure continue to challenge national control.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain important to major transport and energy projects. Debt-service obligations and project performance constrain Kampala's bargaining flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Western, Chinese, and Gulf-linked investors are competing for copper and cobalt assets, giving Zambia leverage but also increasing pressure for favorable concessions. The government is seeking greater local processing and fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and dependence on regional transport corridors limit Zambia's ability to capture more value from mining. Grid investment and corridor diversification remain vulnerable to external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Critical-Mineral Control
frictionVectors.details: Harare is tightening export and processing rules to retain more value from lithium and other minerals. Foreign capital, technology, and market access still leave the sector exposed to external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions, and limited access to international finance weaken the state's ability to invest in mining infrastructure. This increases reliance on opaque bilateral deals and politically connected investors.
